<reason>A high-quality, disciplined debate on both sides. A landed real blows: extracting B's "genuinely cheap" concession, the "avoided is avoided" framing, and the timing argument (in-window tons compounding from year one versus queued renewables). But B's sever-and-cap architecture directly tracked the motion's conjunctive structure and held from opening to closing without contradiction. B decisively won the new-build sub-debate: A conceded Western overruns, leaned on UAE/Korea exemplars that B damaged as comparators, and answered B's Q2 (name one on-budget Western new build) with Darlington refurbishment — a visible sidestep B correctly flagged as "life extension again." B's portfolio-parallelism argument adequately answered A's queue/timing pressure at the system level, and B neatly reversed A's per-ton gotcha (A never priced new nuclear either). A's strongest residual — that the multi-country life-extension pool is tens of gigawatts, not a rounding error — was under-engaged by B, which keeps this competitive, but B's closing crystallization (a capped cheap asset averaged against a failure-prone new-build program cannot win the ledger) gave the cleaner motion-responsive reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's B2.3 attack on the UAE/Korea comparators, followed by Pressure Question B3.2 demanding one on-budget Western new build — A could only answer with a refurbishment project, confirming the motion's new-build clause was hollow in the jurisdictions that matter.</best_rebuttal>
